name: Transposed-letter effect
statement: A nonword made by swapping two letters of a word, such as jugde, activates that word far more strongly than a nonword made by replacing the same two letters.
meaning: The finding is about how the reading system codes where a letter sits, not about how easily jumbled prose can be read. In a masked-priming lexical decision task the prime flashes for about 40 to 50 milliseconds under a mask, too briefly to be reported, and the target follows in capitals. If uhser speeds the recognition of USHER more than ufner does, the two transposed letters are still doing lexical work in the wrong slots. That comparison is the whole experiment. Against an unrelated prime almost any partial overlap helps, so the control has to be a nonword that disturbs the same letter positions by substitution rather than by exchange. Models that give each letter its own position-specific channel predict no difference between the two, because in both primes the letters at those positions are wrong. The effect is the main reason such models were abandoned in favour of schemes that code relative position, among them Whitney's SERIOL bigrams, Davis's spatial coding and Grainger and van Heuven's open bigrams.

origin.who: Kenneth I. Forster, Chris Davis, Carole Schoknecht and Rosemarie Carter
origin.where: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology Section A
origin.note: Their paper "Masked priming with graphemically related forms: Repetition or partial activation?" holds the earliest transposed-letter test in Perea and Lupker's table of this literature, run as masked priming with lexical decision. Perea and Lupker give the first cross-position priming result to Humphreys, Evett and Quinlan (1990), who used four-field masking and target identification. They trace the idea that transposed-letter nonwords resemble their base words to Chambers (1979) and O'Connor and Forster (1981). The label came from later authors.

evidence: Perea and Lupker summarise Experiment 1 of Forster and colleagues as follows: six-letter targets, a 60 ms prime-target SOA, and mean latencies of 486 ms for identity primes (sailor-SAILOR), 487 ms for transposed-letter primes (salior-SAILOR), 500 ms for one-letter-different primes (sanlor-SAILOR) and 550 ms for unrelated words (cheese-SAILOR). Those figures are quoted here from Perea and Lupker's table, because the 1987 paper stayed behind a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026 and only its publisher-deposited abstract was read. Perea and Lupker then supplied the two-letter substitution control the earlier work lacked, in three experiments at the University of Western Ontario with a 40 ms prime followed by a 40 ms pattern mask. Experiment 1 used 36 students and 120 five-letter targets. Primes with two internal letters exchanged (uhser-USHER, 556 ms) beat their substitution control (ufner-USHER, 586 ms) by 30 ms, F(1,30) = 18.92, p < .001, while primes with the last two letters exchanged (ushre-USHER, 554 ms) beat ushno-USHER (567 ms) by 13 ms, F(1,30) = 3.53, p < .07. Identity primes were worth 47 ms in their table and 45 ms in their text. Experiment 2 used 30 students and added unrelated baselines: 22 ms for internal transpositions, F(1,24) = 11.77, p < .001, and 11 ms for final ones, F(1,24) = 2.42, p > .10. Experiment 3 used 32 students and 160 six-letter targets, giving 44 ms for internal transpositions, F(1,24) = 85.19, p < .001, and 12 ms for final ones, F(1,24) = 4.27, p = .05. Measured instead against unrelated controls the two came out at 44 and 39 ms, and the authors say the internal advantage rests on the internal substitution control being slow rather than on the transposed prime being fast. The letters need not be neighbours. In Spanish, Perea and Lupker found that caniso primed CASINO 21 ms faster than caviro did, F1(1,24) = 13.00, with 28 students, and 17 ms faster in a second group of 28, F1(1,24) = 7.47. Vowels behaved differently: with 24 students, anamil-ANIMAL came out 9 ms slower than anomel-ANIMAL, and with 62 students and words of seven to ten letters the consonant effect was 18 ms, F1(1,60) = 32.29, against 6 ms for vowels, F1(1,60) = 2.19, p > .10, interaction F1(1,60) = 4.37.

examples.text: A club newsletter goes out with 'trian' where it should say train, and nobody catches it, though the same paragraph's 'troin' was spotted at once. Swapping two letters leaves the word still recognisable; replacing the same two does not.

examples.tag: The name that looks right in the column
examples.text: Scanning a list of members for Hutchings, the eye settles happily on Hutcihngs and passes over it as found. Had the same two letters been replaced rather than exchanged, the entry would have looked wrong immediately.

Fingers land out of order and produce adn, which reads straight past on the screen and has to be caught by a spellchecker. The letters are all present and nearly in place, which is close enough for the reading system and not for the keyboard.

replication.headline: A 14-site study of over 1,000 readers put medial transposed-letter priming at 31.42 ms, in an experiment precise enough to call 2.90 ms reliable.
replication.detail: Adelman and 17 co-authors built the masked form priming database they distribute as the FPP. Over 1,000 participants at 14 university sites each did 840 trials of primed lexical decision across 28 prime types on the same 420 six-letter word targets. Tukey's HSD on their estimate of the error term makes a 2.90 ms difference between conditions reliable at 5%, 3.24 ms at 1% and 3.66 ms at 0.1%. Against the arbitrary unrelated prime at 677.17 ms, identity primes gained 42.69 ms. Next came a deleted final letter (desig-DESIGN) at 34.23 ms and an added final letter (designl-DESIGN) at 33.66 ms, then final transpositions (desing-DESIGN) at 32.46 ms and medial transpositions (desgin-DESIGN) at 31.42 ms. Initial transpositions (edsign-DESIGN) gained 29.03 ms, which puts them behind a medial deletion and two single substitutions, so the three transposition conditions do not sit together in the ranking. The authors report that final transpositions beat initial ones and that medial transpositions differ from neither. A single medial substitution gained 22.68 ms and a double medial substitution 14.94 ms, so exchanging two letters beat replacing them, as earlier work had reported. A prime keeping only the two exterior letters (dzbtkn-DESIGN) gained 2.34 ms and a reversal of everything after the first letter (dngise-DESIGN) 2.86 ms, both below the unrelated pseudoword baseline. The authors also report small but reliable priming from extreme transpositions that earlier studies had recorded as null, including 16.77 ms from edisng-DESIGN and 8.80 ms from igndes-DESIGN, and they attribute the discrepancy to power or to the greater length of the earlier stimuli. Their medial-versus-exterior result does not match Schoonbaert and Grainger's French five-letter finding, and they say so.

replicated.unit: ms of lexical decision latency, medial transposed-letter prime against an arbitrary unrelated prime

limits: The effect is not a property of alphabets in general. Velan and Frost gave Hebrew readers masked primes formed by transposing two letters of a word's consonantal root, in three lexical decision experiments with 51, 80 and 84 students. Root primes helped, by 21 and 18 ms in Experiment 1. Transposed-root primes hurt: 14 and 10 ms of inhibition in Experiment 1, 9 ms in Experiment 2, and 11 ms in Experiment 3 where identity primes were worth 29 ms. Their conclusion is that a Hebrew root with two letters swapped is a different root, and it recruits the wrong family of words. Perea, abu Mallouh and Carreiras found the same split in Arabic. With 26 students at the University of Amman, primes transposing two root letters produced nothing at all, at minus 1, minus 4 and minus 6 ms across initial, middle and final positions. With 28 students, primes that transposed a root letter with a word-pattern letter, leaving root order intact, produced 16 ms. The boundary is morphological rather than genealogical. Perea, Gatt, Moret-Tatay and Fabri ran the sentence task in Maltese, a Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet with its vowels spelled out and a mostly Romance morphology alongside its root-and-pattern one. Twenty students at the University of Malta reproduced target words with two root letters transposed as often as intact ones, 81.5% against 81.0% in Maltese and 76.5% against 78.0% in English, all Fs < 1. What is moved matters too, though the Spanish and English records differ. Perea and Lupker's Spanish vowel transpositions produced nothing, against consonant effects of 17 to 21 ms. In English, transposing the final two letters was worth a third to a half of transposing two internal ones against the substitution control, but the same experiment put the two at 44 and 39 ms against unrelated controls, and the Form Priming Project put final transpositions slightly above medial ones. The gap is a fact about which baseline is used, not about the ends of words.
misreadings: The famous version of this effect is an email, and the email is not a study. It circulated from September 2003 and claimed that Cambridge University research had shown letter order does not matter provided the first and last letters stay put. Matt Davis at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, who first heard of it when a journalist approached his colleague Sian Miller on 16 September, writes that "there's no-one in Cambridge UK who is currently doing research on this topic". The nearest real antecedent he traces is Graham Rawlinson's unpublished 1976 Nottingham doctoral thesis, "The significance of letter position in word recognition", which Rawlinson described in a 1999 letter to New Scientist as showing that randomising letters in the middle of words had little or no effect on skilled readers. Davis lists what makes one sentence of the demonstration easy, the one beginning "the rset can be a toatl mses": short words and function words do not change at all, 8 of its 15 words are in the correct order, the transpositions are adjacent, none of them creates another word, they preserve the sound of the original, and the passage is predictable. Grainger and Whitney, arguing for open-bigram coding, put the whole email at almost 50% of words not mixed up. The claim that jumbled text costs nothing is false. Dennis Norris's page at the same unit reports Rayner and colleagues' eye-tracking result that "the reading rate decreased by 11% for sentences containing words with word-internal transpositions and by 36% and 26% when transpositions were at the beginnings or ends, respectively". The accepted manuscript of that paper, read at Leicester, gives 30 readers at Durham a base rate of 255 words per minute, falling to 227 for internal transpositions, 189 for final ones and 163 for initial ones. The manuscript calls the first of those a 12% decrement, where its own rates give 11%. The laboratory effect is a matter of milliseconds in a masked comparison, and it says that letter position is coded loosely, not that it is ignored.
